newsitem.title: USA: First-class meals to make it to the poor for a day.
newsitem.headline: First-class meals to make it to the poor for a day.

text.p: First-class restaurants across the country were preparing thousands of Thanksgiving turkeys Wednesday, ready to provide free dinners to the homeless and hungry.
Long lines were expected for the hot meals that soup kitchen workers and volunteers will serve.

"We serve 11,000 meals a year," said Rev. Howard McLendon, who runs Project Manna from the Massachusetts Avenue Baptist Church in Cambridge. "And we've noticed growth in one area in particular -- the number of poor families just keeps growing."

The Charles Hotel in Cambridge and its Culinary Institute of America trained executive chef Peter Davis will provide Project Manna with 150 full-course turkey dinners with all the trimmings for Thursday's feast.

"We started the prepping Tuesday," said Davis, who estimated he will have 20 cooks working to peal the 100 pounds of potatoes, 30 pounds of parsnips, turnips, carrots and celery root, and baste 75 pounds of turkey for the meals that volunteers at the church will serve.
"It's sort of a planned attack," he said. "We're also planning to serve 700 to 800 Thanksgiving Day dinners to our regular patrons."

In Boston, Le Meridien Hotel and the Top of the Hub restaurant are among the eateries that have baked 8,000 pies for Community Servings, an AIDS food service group, which plans to distribute the pecan, apple and pumpkin desserts to their clients.
And in Hartford, Connecticut, the upscale Hastings Hotel, where President Clinton stayed after his debate with Bob Dole, will host its first-ever Thanksgiving feast for the homeless on Nov. 27.
The Hastings, known for its huge ballroom, is owned by insurance giant Aetna and is expecting 200 to 400 people to attend the free dinner, according to a spokesman.
"What's unusual about this event is that we're bringing the guests to the meal, as opposed to bringing the meal to the guests," said the Aetna spokesman Sam Stuart.
Invitations to the dinner were posted at all of the city's homeless shelters and a local transportation company has agreed to a shuttle between the shelters and the hotel.
But it is not just top eateries and hotels that are trying to help this holiday season. Entertainment spots are also donating meals - and a few laughs.

In Hollywood, California, the Laugh Factory will continue its traditional holiday dinner with four seatings Thursday for those in the entertainment industry who could use a boost. The meal is free, but reservations are required for the turkey dinner that is served with a healthy portion of comedy.
In America's heartland, the rotary club in Elmhurst, Illinois, said it expected between 300 and 400 needy people at a special Thanksgiving meal it will serve at the local banquet hall.

But the Rev. McLendon in Cambridge noted, "Thanksgiving is only one day of the year. The need persists year round. And the philanthropic institutions aren't what I like to call hard wired for the long haul. Ten years ago, every one got on the bandwagon. But the problem hasn't gone a way. It's gotten worse."
